It retains the only dedicated technical capability responsible for resolving complex intranet and SharePoint issues, managing global incidents, supporting GDPR and other legal or compliance-related changes, and maintaining a business-critical global employee platform.
 
The intranet protects at least €720,000 in annual employee-productivity value through faster access to information, tools and relevant content.
 
This is based on a deliberately conservative assumption:
60,000 employees save one minute per month
This equals 1,000 hours saved per month
At a fully loaded hourly cost of €60, this represents €60,000 per month
Annual value: €720,000
This calculation excludes further value created through self-service publishing, workflow automation, reduced operational support, personalized performance dashboards, enterprise communications, knowledge sharing and brand consistency.
 
The intranet is a key control for making required employee information available through a single, controlled and auditable global channel. This includes whistleblowing routes, AI and cybersecurity requirements, pay criteria, employment-related policies, and country-specific content required by local laws and regulations.
 
The dedicated development capacity is also needed to implement legal and regulatory changes in the platform. This includes creating or updating targeted pages and applying audience targeting so that content is available only to the relevant countries, employee groups or markets where required. For example, changes in local employment, diversity and inclusion, or other regulatory requirements may require rapid updates to content, access or visibility.
 
It also supports the management of SharePoint incidents, such as potential personal-data exposure, inappropriate access to content or other GDPR-related issues. Without this capability, Philips risks fragmented local communication, inconsistent implementation across countries and a reduced ability to demonstrate that required information was available to the right employees.
 
The intranet does not replace formal training, acknowledgement or case-management systems. It provides the trusted, governed employee-facing gateway that supports them.
 
The potential regulatory exposure is significant. Depending on applicability and national implementation, NIS2 can require maximum administrative fines of at least €10 million or 2% of global annual turnover for essential entities; whistleblowing obligations are enforced through national law; and EU pay-transparency rules can shift the burden of proof in equal-pay claims.
 
Without this dedicated capacity, Philips would face:
Longer resolution times for complex intranet and SharePoint defects, resulting in degraded user experience and disruption for employees.
No established specialist owner for global SharePoint incidents, increasing response times and business impact.
Delayed or stopped improvements to employee experience, automation, accessibility, performance and dashboards, while the backlog continues to grow.
Delayed content-lifecycle and governance work, increasing compliance risk and future remediation effort.
Delayed implementation of regulatory or legal changes, including required country-specific pages and targeted content.
A weaker intranet as the central gateway to the digital employee experience, resulting in fragmented journeys, continued manual work and reduced trust in the platform.
Less reliable access to relevant business information and personalized performance data, weakening strategic alignment.
Loss of accumulated platform knowledge, requiring supplier re-onboarding, discovery and knowledge transfer before delivery could restart in the future.
 
The decision is not between spending and saving €175,000. It is between retaining the dedicated technical capability for Philips’ global employee platform and accepting at least €720,000 in annual productivity value at risk, together with slower incident resolution, growing operational and compliance risk, and loss of a trusted digital gateway for employees.

Less reliable access to relevant business information and personalized performance data, weakening strategic alignment. The 2025–2026 replatforming (about €1.9M) went live as a minimum viable product (MVP) to switch off the old platform (AEM) on time: pages and templates work, but legal controls and features the business case relied on were deferred because of budget and timeline. Each legal gap below was raised by Legal, Privacy Legal, External Relations or a country team. A. Legal and regulatory gaps 1. Timed, market-sensitive releases depend on PAL (Philips' image and document library). Quarterly and annual results press releases and other time-critical announcements (e.g. acquisitions, divestments, bonds) are timed to the minute; External Relations: some releases must be online within 25–30 minutes to meet regulatory obligations. Yet every file (e.g. the press release PDF) must go through PAL: an upload can take up to 30 minutes, and a replaced file can take hours to show on the live site. There is no back-up: files cannot be uploaded directly in Contentful, which is a hard requirement for regulated releases. Embargoed files are exposed too: a draft PDF or image can be opened via a direct PAL link before release (requirements for a restricted PAL area went to IT on 22 Sep 2026; IT is now scoping it – no solution or estimate yet). Result: files go live too early or too late. From the Q4 2026 results, results publication moves from the Results Hub to philips.com (see EW-176), so this hits the regulated release itself. What is at stake showed on 27 July 2026, when the Q2 results went live early via the Results Hub: a 30-minute trading halt and formal AFM and SEC filings. 2. No approval workflow: the MVP delivered templates and components, but no approval workflows are built in yet. Content goes live without a second approval, while country teams now publish themselves (self-service). External Relations requires approval workflows (8 Sep 2026). This governance is critical: without it, content can go live unintended or too early – damaging Philips' reputation, or releasing market-sensitive information before its time. 3. Privacy notice pages: Privacy Legal requires each privacy notice as one page on the global domain with all languages and a language selector. The new platform has no such set-up – it builds one page per locale. The page also does not show the visitor's country, so the required country-specific privacy information (e.g. US, Japan, Taiwan, Turkey, China, Brazil, EEA) is missing. Privacy Legal: "This is a requirement." Some locales have no working terms of use (e.g. Slovenia, Belarus). 4. Country rules the templates cannot meet. Italy: a legally required notice (medical-device content is for journalists and healthcare professionals only) can only be switched on or off for a whole section, and required wording (Legislative Decree 231/2001) does not fit the component. Russia: words break mid-word (also in English), so Executive Committee and Supervisory Board information is hidden. Canada: the required accessibility (AODA) and forced-labour pages are still on the old platform. 5. EU AI Act (transparency rules from 2 August 2026): Legal's AI-Act changes to the terms of use must reach all 90+ local sites, and AI-generated images and content need visible, screen-reader and machine-readable labels. More work is expected once Legal finalises its guidance. B. Finish what we started The MVP delivered the switch-off, not yet the value. A2. Approval workflows and publishing rights (governance): approval workflows built into Contentful – a recorded second approval before anything goes live (four-eyes principle); a stricter flow with sign-off by the content owner (e.g. External Relations, Investor Relations, Legal) for market-sensitive and legal pages; publishing and scheduling only after approval; role-based publishing rights for country publishers; an audit trail of who approved what and when (also evidence of human review for AI-assisted content under the AI Act); and flagging of rights-restricted, single-use images in PAL (e.g. a partner CEO photo) to prevent unlicensed reuse. A3. Privacy and legal notice set-up: each privacy notice (Philips-wide and app notices) as one page on the global domain with all languages and a language selector, showing the country section that applies to the visitor; complete terms of use and cookie notices for every locale; removal of outdated notices; stable addresses for legally referenced documents; complete 5-year archive of regulated announcements. A4. A5. A6. Compliance assurance: every change validated under the website's quality process (releases are QMS-assessed) with Legal sign-off. B. The 2025–2026 replatforming (about €1.9M) went live as a minimum viable product (MVP) to switch off the old platform (AEM) on time: pages and templates work, but legal controls and features the business case relied on were deferred because of budget and timeline. Each legal gap below was raised by Legal, Privacy Legal, External Relations or a country team.

A. Legal and regulatory gaps
1. Timed, market-sensitive releases depend on PAL (Philips' image and document library). Quarterly and annual results press releases and other time-critical announcements (e.g. acquisitions, divestments, bonds) are timed to the minute; External Relations: some releases must be online within 25–30 minutes to meet regulatory obligations. Yet every file (e.g. the press release PDF) must go through PAL: an upload can take up to 30 minutes, and a replaced file can take hours to show on the live site. There is no back-up: files cannot be uploaded directly in Contentful, which is a hard requirement for regulated releases. Embargoed files are exposed too: a draft PDF or image can be opened via a direct PAL link before release (requirements for a restricted PAL area went to IT on 22 Sep 2026; IT is now scoping it – no solution or estimate yet). Result: files go live too early or too late. From the Q4 2026 results, results publication moves from the Results Hub to philips.com (see EW-176), so this hits the regulated release itself. What is at stake showed on 27 July 2026, when the Q2 results went live early via the Results Hub: a 30-minute trading halt and formal AFM and SEC filings.
2. No approval workflow: the MVP delivered templates and components, but no approval workflows are built in yet. Content goes live without a second approval, while country teams now publish themselves (self-service). External Relations requires approval workflows (8 Sep 2026). This governance is critical: without it, content can go live unintended or too early – damaging Philips' reputation, or releasing market-sensitive information before its time. 
3. Privacy notice pages: Privacy Legal requires each privacy notice as one page on the global domain with all languages and a language selector. The new platform has no such set-up – it builds one page per locale. The page also does not show the visitor's country, so the required country-specific privacy information (e.g. US, Japan, Taiwan, Turkey, China, Brazil, EEA) is missing. Privacy Legal: "This is a requirement." Some locales have no working terms of use (e.g. Slovenia, Belarus).
4. Country rules the templates cannot meet. Italy: a legally required notice (medical-device content is for journalists and healthcare professionals only) can only be switched on or off for a whole section, and required wording (Legislative Decree 231/2001) does not fit the component. Russia: words break mid-word (also in English), so Executive Committee and Supervisory Board information is hidden. Canada: the required accessibility (AODA) and forced-labour pages are still on the old platform.
5. EU AI Act (transparency rules from 2 August 2026): Legal's AI-Act changes to the terms of use must reach all 90+ local sites, and AI-generated images and content need visible, screen-reader and machine-readable labels. More work is expected once Legal finalises its guidance.

B. Finish what we started
The MVP delivered the switch-off, not yet the value. Features were deferred (e.g. advanced media library, experience improvements, GEO / AI findability  enhancements), testing coverage is limited (2026 releases caused download and language defects) and there is no funded aftercare (no January release planned). Without completion, the replatforming does not deliver its business case.","formula":"=IF('[1]Functions, Regions, C&S'!AH160="","",'[1]Functions, Regions, C&S'!AH160)"},{"label":"Scope / Free text [AI]","value":"2027 scope – A. legal controls (Priority 1) and B. completion of the replatforming (carry-over):

A2. Approval workflows and publishing rights (governance): approval workflows built into Contentful – a recorded second approval before anything goes live (four-eyes principle); a stricter flow with sign-off by the content owner (e.g. External Relations, Investor Relations, Legal) for market-sensitive and legal pages; publishing and scheduling only after approval; role-based publishing rights for country publishers; an audit trail of who approved what and when (also evidence of human review for AI-assisted content under the AI Act); and flagging of rights-restricted, single-use images in PAL (e.g. a partner CEO photo) to prevent unlicensed reuse.
A3. Privacy and legal notice set-up: each privacy notice (Philips-wide and app notices) as one page on the global domain with all languages and a language selector, showing the country section that applies to the visitor; complete terms of use and cookie notices for every locale; removal of outdated notices; stable addresses for legally referenced documents; complete 5-year archive of regulated announcements.
A4. Country legal requirements: legal notices and pop-ups set per page and per country (Italy first); components that can hold mandatory legal wording; correct line breaks in all languages (Russia first); Canada AODA and forced-labour pages.

A6. Compliance assurance: every change validated under the website's quality process (releases are QMS-assessed) with Legal sign-off.
B. Software Transformation

3PP/Keystone Re-platforming
Re-platform the current 3PP (3rd Party Procurement) onboarding and management solution to a scalable, Philips IT-landscape tool fit, enabling end-to-end workflow simplification, improved user experience, and stronger compliance while supporting future growth of 3PP business.

Cost Master
Enhance cost intelligence capabilities in Direct Procurement through: 
•	Enhancement of existing Cost Master capabilities (Library connection): Upgrade and maintain the Cost Master Library, enabling automated price updates and seamless integration with SMRS and Windchill 
•	Deployment of AI-driven should-cost solution (new Should cost calculation tool): Implement a cloud based, AI-enabled should-costing tool (e.g. TrueValueHub) to replace the existing local DFMA tool
•	Sustainment of market intelligence data (databases): Ensure continued access to commodity and component cost databases (e.g. MySteel, Nexar, Beroe, MetalMiner, Fastmarkets)

Risk Management
Build a centralized N-tier supplier risk monitoring capability to address the current lack of visibility beyond Tier-1 suppliers. It retains the only dedicated technical capability responsible for resolving complex intranet and SharePoint issues, managing global incidents, supporting GDPR and other legal or compliance-related changes, and maintaining a business-critical global employee platform.
 
The intranet protects at least €720,000 in annual employee-productivity value through faster access to information, tools and relevant content.
 
This is based on a deliberately conservative assumption:
60,000 employees save one minute per month
This equals 1,000 hours saved per month
At a fully loaded hourly cost of €60, this represents €60,000 per month
Annual value: €720,000
This calculation excludes further value created through self-service publishing, workflow automation, reduced operational support, personalized performance dashboards, enterprise communications, knowledge sharing and brand consistency.
 
The intranet is a key control for making required employee information available through a single, controlled and auditable global channel. This includes whistleblowing routes, AI and cybersecurity requirements, pay criteria, employment-related policies, and country-specific content required by local laws and regulations.
 
The dedicated development capacity is also needed to implement legal and regulatory changes in the platform. This includes creating or updating targeted pages and applying audience targeting so that content is available only to the relevant countries, employee groups or markets where required. For example, changes in local employment, diversity and inclusion, or other regulatory requirements may require rapid updates to content, access or visibility.
 
It also supports the management of SharePoint incidents, such as potential personal-data exposure, inappropriate access to content or other GDPR-related issues. Without this capability, Philips risks fragmented local communication, inconsistent implementation across countries and a reduced ability to demonstrate that required information was available to the right employees.
 
The intranet does not replace formal training, acknowledgement or case-management systems. It provides the trusted, governed employee-facing gateway that supports them.
 
The potential regulatory exposure is significant. Depending on applicability and national implementation, NIS2 can require maximum administrative fines of at least €10 million or 2% of global annual turnover for essential entities; whistleblowing obligations are enforced through national law; and EU pay-transparency rules can shift the burden of proof in equal-pay claims.
 
Without this dedicated capacity, Philips would face:
Longer resolution times for complex intranet and SharePoint defects, resulting in degraded user experience and disruption for employees.
No established specialist owner for global SharePoint incidents, increasing response times and business impact.
Delayed or stopped improvements to employee experience, automation, accessibility, performance and dashboards, while the backlog continues to grow.
Delayed content-lifecycle and governance work, increasing compliance risk and future remediation effort.
Delayed implementation of regulatory or legal changes, including required country-specific pages and targeted content.
A weaker intranet as the central gateway to the digital employee experience, resulting in fragmented journeys, continued manual work and reduced trust in the platform.
Less reliable access to relevant business information and personalized performance data, weakening strategic alignment.
Loss of accumulated platform knowledge, requiring supplier re-onboarding, discovery and knowledge transfer before delivery could restart in the future.
 
The decision is not between spending and saving €175,000. It is between retaining the dedicated technical capability for Philips’ global employee platform and accepting at least €720,000 in annual productivity value at risk, together with slower incident resolution, growing operational and compliance risk, and loss of a trusted digital gateway for employees.
 
Beyond the quantified value, the investment enables more consistent enterprise communications, faster business-change implementation, stronger knowledge sharing, personalized performance dashboards, and a coherent Philips employee experience across connected digital touchpoints.","1 year","Must Do",null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,"The global SharePoint intranet is the centre of Philips’ digital employee experience and the central gateway through which approximately 70,000 employees access trusted information, business updates, digital tools, enterprise communications and personalized performance dashboards.
The intranet is not a static communications site. While standard SharePoint capabilities support basic publishing, Philips requires dedicated technical expertise to deliver and maintain tailored functionality, integrations, automation, performance improvements, accessibility, governance and content lifecycle management. A. Legal and regulatory gaps

The page also does not show the visitor's country, so the required country-specific privacy information (e.g. US, Japan, Taiwan, Turkey, China, Brazil, EEA) is missing. Privacy Legal: "This is a requirement." Some locales have no working terms of use (e.g. Slovenia, Belarus).
4. Country rules the templates cannot meet. Russia: words break mid-word (also in English), so Executive Committee and Supervisory Board information is hidden. Canada: the required accessibility (AODA) and forced-labour pages are still on the old platform.
5. EU AI Act (transparency rules from 2 August 2026): Legal's AI-Act changes to the terms of use must reach all 90+ local sites, and AI-generated images and content need visible, screen-reader and machine-readable labels. More work is expected once Legal finalises its guidance.
